title: DFS on Lisbon: Real Streets, Deep Backtracking ⚡
description: Watch Depth-First Search (DFS) “dive” through Lisbon’s Alfama streets like a stack-powered explorer. Each step marks visited intersections, and when DFS hits a dead-end, it backtracks along the exact route it chose.
ig_caption:
Depth First Search (DFS) Traversal on Real Street Maps — What happens when DFS explores real city intersections ⚡

In this visualization, every street intersection becomes a node and every road segment becomes an edge. DFS uses a last-in, first-out stack behavior (conceptually like recursion + call stack):
• It picks a neighbor and goes as deep as possible
• It marks nodes visited to prevent cycles
• When it can’t go further, it backtracks to the last branching point

That “deep dive then retreat” is why DFS can look dramatic on real maps—especially in dense areas with loops.

✅ Takeaway: DFS is great for exploring reachable areas and building paths in graphs, but traversal order (neighbor sorting) can change the route you see.

Debate question: If two streets are both “equally close,” should the DFS choose the one with the shortest heuristic—or just the one that appears first in your neighbor list?
